lesson.title: Berufe II: der Student, der Fahrer, der Sänger, der Bauer, der Arbeiter
lesson.subtitle: the -er jobs do what English -er does — and Bauer turns out to be the dweller inside neighbor

hook.title: The -er Machine, and One Family Reunion
hook.content: Three of today's jobs are the -er machine running on verbs you already own. der Fahrer is fahren + -er — and fahren is English fare: the same verb that survives in wayfarer and seafarer, so a Fahrer is literally a farer, one who fares. der Sänger is singen + -er, and singen is sing wearing its full ablaut — singen, sang, gesungen against sing, sang, sung: the same seven vowel steps in the same order, the strongest evidence on the course that these two languages are one verb system. der Student is the Latin import: studieren was already yours (Latin studēre, 'to study'), and der Student is that verb's person — Latin made the noun out of the present participle, 'the one studying'. Then the family gem: der Bauer is the -er of bauen, which originally meant not to build but to dwell. A Bauer is a dweller — and English kept the same dweller-word twice: in neighbor, the old near-dweller (nigh + bur), and in boor, the bare dweller that became an insult. Farmer, neighbor and boor are one word at three distances. der Arbeiter is the honest one: die Arbeit has no English cognate — English lost whatever twin it had, and work's true German twin is Werk, a different word entirely.

footnotes.title: The -in Keeps the List Honest
footnotes.content: German marks the women of these jobs with -in: die Sängerin, die Arbeiterin, die Studentin, die Fahrerin. The -er names the job; the -in names the person who holds it. Bäckerin and Verkäuferin from the last lesson work the same way.

pattern.title: The Doer in the Sentence
pattern.content: 1. The agent does the verb: Der Fahrer fährt den Bus — fahren in slot 2 with its vowel change, der Student studiert, der Sänger singt. 2. Professions stay bare after sein, as in the last lesson: Der Mann ist Student. 3. Where they stand: Der Bauer wohnt im Dorf — dwelling verbs (wohnen) pair naturally with dwelling people. 4. Plurals: der Sänger → die Sänger, der Fahrer → die Fahrer (-er stays), but der Student → die Studenten — the Latin import takes the Latin-style -en ending.
pattern.linguist_note: sing/sang/sung and singen/sang/gesungen are not similar — they are the same ablaut row, inherited whole from Proto-Germanic. Vowel change as grammar (here: past tense) predates both languages, which is why a German learner's strongest anchor is not a word list but the vowel map English already ships with. Bauer's row is different evidence: not a shared verb system but one noun that split into dweller, farmer, neighbor and boor as the languages drifted apart.

exercises.prompt: The -er jobs — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: The farmer lives in the village
The worker comes at seven o'clock
matching_pairs.german: Der Arbeiter kommt um sieben Uhr

matching_pairs.english: The worker wears trousers and a shirt
matching_pairs.german: Der Arbeiter trägt eine Hose und ein Hemd

matching_pairs.english: In winter the farmer wears a coat, a scarf, a hat and warm socks
matching_pairs.german: Im Winter trägt der Bauer einen Mantel, einen Schal, einen Hut und warme Socken

matching_pairs.english: The student wears a jacket today
matching_pairs.german: Der Student trägt heute eine Jacke

matching_pairs.english: The driver reads the timetable and drives to Poland
matching_pairs.german: Der Fahrer liest den Fahrplan und fährt nach Polen

matching_pairs.english: The farmer brings meat, cheese and vegetables
matching_pairs.german: Der Bauer bringt Fleisch, Käse und Gemüse

matching_pairs.english: The farmer sells potatoes, cucumbers and onions
matching_pairs.german: Der Bauer verkauft Kartoffeln, Gurken und Zwiebeln

exercises.target_answer: Der Student ist jung, Der Bauer wohnt im Dorf, Der Sänger singt schön, Der Arbeiter kommt um sieben Uhr, Der Fahrer fährt den Bus, Der Arbeiter trägt eine Hose und ein Hemd, Im Winter trägt der Bauer einen Mantel, einen Schal, einen Hut und warme Socken, Der Student trägt heute eine Jacke, Der Fahrer liest den Fahrplan und fährt nach Polen, Der Polizist fragt den Studenten, Der Bauer bringt Fleisch, Käse und Gemüse, Der Bauer verkauft Kartoffeln, Gurken und Zwiebeln
exercises.meaning: be young, live in the village, sing, come at seven, drive the bus
exercises.explanation: Every job word does its own verb: the Sänger singt, the Fahrer fährt (vowel change), the Bauer wohnt. Note fährt's vowel — the same ablaut family that turns singen into sang.

exercises.prompt: singen – sang – gesungen ↔ sing – sang – sung: the same ablaut, step for step. Which job word is built on that verb?
exercises.meaning: der Sänger ← singen: the strong-verb job
exercises.explanation: der Sänger is singen's doer — and the vowel inside Sänger (ä) is the plural/stem echo of the same verb. der Fahrer's verb changes its vowel too (fährt), but it is fahren/fare, a different strong verb.

exercises.prompt: der Bauer is the dweller (bauen, originally 'to dwell'). English kept the same dweller-word in neighbor, the near-dweller — and once more, bare. Which English word is Bauer's twin?
exercises.explanation: boor is the same dweller-word as Bauer (English took it through Dutch boer): the country person, later an insult. boar is the pig — a different root that happens to look close; bore and bourgeois are unrelated. The full family: Bauer the farmer, neighbor the near-dweller, boor the bare one.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'The student studies in the city'
exercises.target_answer: Der Student studiert in der Stadt
exercises.meaning: The student studies in the city
exercises.explanation: der Student studiert — the Latin import and its verb are one family, exactly like Fahrer/fahren. in der Stadt takes the dative the way in der Schweiz did; der Stadt is die Stadt in its dative dress.

vocab_hints.note: the verb behind der Fahrer — and the twin of English fare (wayfarer, seafarer). nach takes the destination: nach Italien, nach Deutschland.

exercises.explanation: Wir fahren nach Italien — the verb that names the driver. The bank keeps der Fahrer and der Auto-world nearby to make the point: whoever fährt is the Fahrer; the -er is waiting on the verb.

summary.outcome: Name the -er jobs, hear singen's ablaut inside Sänger, use them with their own verbs, and recite Bauer's family: farmer, neighbor, boor.

use_example.german: Der Sänger singt schön — der Fahrer fährt den Bus.
use_example.english: The singer sings beautifully — the driver drives the bus.

summary.takeaway: -er does English -er's work on both sides; singen-sang-gesungen mirrors sing-sang-sung; Bauer is the dweller in neighbor and boor; Student is studēre's person; Arbeit has no English twin — work's twin is Werk.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the borrowed row — der Ingenieur, der Friseur, der Pilot, der Kellner — and der Beruf, which is vocation translated rather than inherited.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Berufe II: der Student, der Fahrer, der Sänger, der Bauer, der Arbeiter (We are driving to Italy):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Wir fahren nach Italien" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Berufe II: der Student, der Fahrer, der Sänger, der Bauer, der Arbeiter without relying on short-term echo.

student.etymology_derivation: From Medieval Latin studēns — a Latin loan both languages borrowed alike. [wiktionary]

fahrer.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of fahren (to fare/drive) + -er — the fare family again. [wiktionary]

sänger.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of singen (sing); initial s voices to [z] before vowels. [wiktionary]

bauer.context_phrase: Der Bauer wohnt auf dem Hof.
bauer.context_translation: The farmer lives on the farm.
bauer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *būraz "dweller" — cognate with English boor, and with bower "dwelling". [wiktionary]

arbeiter.context_phrase: Der Arbeiter kommt um sieben Uhr.
arbeiter.context_translation: The worker comes at seven o'clock.
arbeiter.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of arbeiten (work) + -er; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

hose.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *hosā — the same Germanic source as English hose (hosiery). [wiktionary]

hemd.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *hamiþi; English shirt is from a different root — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

mantel.etymology_derivation: From Late Latin mantellum, ultimately Gaulish — a Romance loan; no English cognate. [wiktionary]

jacke.etymology_derivation: From Middle French jaque (from the name Jacques) — the same French source as English jacket. [wiktionary]

hut.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hōdaz — Wiktionary's English cognate is hood, not hat. See Fingerhut. [wiktionary]

schal.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from English shawl, from Persian šâl — a loan, not an inherited cognate. [wiktionary]

socke.etymology_derivation: West Germanic borrowing from Latin soccus 'slipper' — a parallel borrowing with English sock. [wiktionary]

hinten.context_translation: The toilet is at the back on the left.
hinten.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *hindanē — the same hind root as English behind and hind; German shifted d to t (the entry points to hinter for the consonantism). [wiktionary]

fahrplan.context_phrase: Der Fahrplan hängt an der Wand.
fahrplan.context_translation: The timetable hangs on the wall.
fahrplan.etymology_derivation: fahren (to drive, the fare root) + Plan (plan, the same French-Latin word English uses): the travel-plan, a timetable. [wiktionary]

polen.etymology_derivation: Middle High German Polen, plural of Pole — land of the Poles. [wiktionary]

polizist.context_phrase: Der Polizist fragt nach dem Weg.
polizist.context_translation: The policeman asks about the way.
polizist.etymology_derivation: Polizei + -ist, from Greek pólis via Latin polītīa — the same loan both languages share. [wiktionary]

sprache.context_phrase: Die Sprache ist schwer zu lernen.
sprache.context_translation: The language is hard to learn.
sprache.etymology_derivation: From Old High German sprāhha, Proto-West Germanic *sprāku, the twin of English speech; the k to ch velar shift links both to the sprechen and speak family. [wiktionary]

fleisch.context_phrase: Ich esse gern Fleisch mit Kartoffeln.
fleisch.context_translation: I like eating meat with potatoes.
fleisch.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *flaiski — the exact counterpart of English flesh. [wiktionary]

käse.context_phrase: Der Käse auf dem Brot ist lecker.
käse.context_translation: The cheese on the bread is tasty.
käse.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *kāsī, borrowed early from Latin cāseus — shared with English cheese. [wiktionary]

gemüse.etymology_derivation: From Old High German muos 'food, porridge'; English mush is only a possible cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

kartoffel.etymology_derivation: From Tartuffel, from Italian tartufolo 'truffle', Latin terrae tūber 'earth tuber'; no English cognate. [wiktionary]

gurke.context_phrase: Die Gurke ist frisch und grün.
gurke.context_translation: The cucumber is fresh and green.
gurke.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Old Polish ogórek, Greek angoúrion — cognate with English gherkin. [wiktionary]

zwiebel.etymology_derivation: Borrowed early from Late Latin cēpulla; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

schüler.etymology_derivation: From Medieval Latin scholaris — the same Latin loan that gave English scholar. [wiktionary]

italien.etymology_derivation: The same Latin name Italia as English Italy; shared proper name, no sound shift to fake. [wiktionary]

singen.etymology_derivation: Initial S voiced to [z] before vowels.

fahren.context_translation: I am going / driving to Berlin.
fahren.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *faraną — the twin of English fare (farewell, bus fare, 'how did you fare?'). [wiktionary]

wohnen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wunāną, from the 'wish, love' root; no English cognate named on Wiktionary. [wiktionary]

dorf.context_phrase: Das Dorf liegt hinter dem Berg.
dorf.context_translation: The village lies behind the mountain.
dorf.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *thurpa — Old English thorp, which survives in English place names like Mablethorpe; the English th hardened into German d. [wiktionary]

bus.context_phrase: Der Bus kommt um acht Uhr.
bus.context_translation: The bus comes at eight o'clock.
bus.etymology_derivation: From Omnibus, the Latin for-all vehicle, shortened with influence from English bus — both languages took the same Latin dative. [wiktionary]

jung.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *jungaz — the twin of English young (see der Junge). [wiktionary]

auto.etymology_derivation: Short for Automobil — the same Greek autos ('self') loan as English auto, clipped German-style. [wiktionary]

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: English and German share the 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels rather than adding endings.
strong_verbs_ablaut.philological_note: Joseph Wright's Historical German Grammar categorizes these 7 classes. Knowing "sing-sang-sung" gives you "singen-sang-gesungen", "drink-drank-drunk" gives you "trinken-trank-getrunken", and "drive-drove-driven" gives you "treiben-trieb-getrieben".
